tasks.short: Decide which tests are due, order them under protocol, run point-of-care tests, interpret results and report.

steps.what: Nurse assesses the patient and decides which diagnostic tests are due under the unit protocol
Nurse prepares the lab orders: one by one in the record today, by one protocol order set selection after the change
Nurse checks the orders before they go: tests, patient, urgency, and which ones fall outside the nurse protocol
Nurse submits the checked orders to the lab, with out-of-protocol orders routed to the intensivist
Intensivist co-signs orders that fall outside the nurse protocol
Nurse draws samples and performs screening procedures at the bedside, such as blood gas and glucose

Nurse records point-of-care results: copied from the analyser printout today; after the change the nurse scans the wristband at the analyser and confirms each imported result sits under the right patient and time
Nurse looks up earlier results across record tabs to compare
Nurse interprets the results against the clinical picture, age and health status
Nurse reports abnormal results to the intensivist and acts under protocol

tasks.design: Configure protocol order sets in the electronic health record ({OTHER}) so the tests a nurse may order are one selection, with out-of-protocol orders routed to the intensivist for co-signing as today. Point-of-care analysers send results to the record after a wristband scan, and a trend view shows each result beside earlier values and reference ranges; interpretation stays with the nurse and intensivist.
tasks.previous_blocker: Analysers printed results that were copied by hand, and earlier values sat in separate record tabs.
tasks.enabler_now: Hospital records support order sets and trend views as configuration, and point-of-care analysers can send results through device middleware.
tasks.still_hard: Interpreting results needs the clinical picture; software that interprets would be a high-risk medical device. Which tests nurses may order depends on protocol.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing which result does not fit the patient in front of them and raising it before it becomes an emergency.

ambition.what: Protocol tests such as glucose and electrolytes ordered by the nurse the moment they are due, not at the next doctor's round.

tasks.altitude: The nurse orders from a set and reads results in one view; ordering rights stay as the protocol defines.

reach.task: Phone critical results to the ward
reach.learn: Whether alerts in the record can safely replace some of the calls.

evidence.claim: Hospital records support protocol order sets and result trend views as configuration, and point-of-care analysers can send results to the record.
AI in medical devices that need a notified body is high-risk under the AI Act, which keeps automated interpretation out of this design.
Which tests a nurse may order without a doctor depends on national rules and hospital protocols.
The medical record is kept twenty years after the last change.

assumptions: Boundary: from deciding a test is due to reporting the result; treatment decisions are outside.

Input contract: order sets built from the unit test protocol kept by the protocol committee; point-of-care results with patient id from the wristband scanned at the analyser by the nurse, sent through the device middleware run by the lab's point-of-care coordinator; fallback is the printout and typing.
Lab results from the central lab already flow to the record; that runtime earns no saving.
Intensivist and lab time is outside the nurse's savings.

Priced here: the answer for sibling task 18308 does not cut copying analyser printouts. With the analyser sending results after a wristband scan, s5 keeps 20, the time the nurse spends confirming that each imported result sits under the right patient and time.
s2 keeps 60 for choosing the order set and adding single tests; the order check (s2b) and submission (s2c) take 1 each. s6 keeps 40 for reading the trend view.
unknowns: Whether the unit's point-of-care analysers are connected to the record.
Which tests the nurse protocol lets nurses order.
research_questions: Do protocol order sets shorten the time from a due test to its result?

already_counted.description: Nurse confirms that imported point-of-care results sit under the right patient and time.

incremental.description: Nurse handles failed analyser uploads and unmatched results.
Point-of-care coordinator keeps device connections working and the protocol committee keeps order sets current.

approvals.approved_version: The lab orders with tests, patient and urgency exactly as checked by the nurse in s2b, submitted once to the lab, with out-of-protocol orders routed to the intensivist for co-signing; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the unit's blood gas analysers already send results, so s5 saves nothing and keeps 100; only order sets and the trend view save time (9.1); high: analysers connected through this change (17.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The acute care nurse keeps assessment, sampling and interpretation; ordering, copying and looking up results shrink.
skills_to_grow: Ordering within protocol from order sets
role.ambitious_version: An acute care nurse who orders due tests on time and sees every result in context without leaving the bedside.
